News.title: Convicted abuser was wearing ANKLE TAG when he ‘murdered TikTok star & dumped body in vineyard’ 600 miles from his home
News.content:
'MURDER' SHOCK Convicted abuser was wearing ANKLE TAG when he ‘murdered TikTok star & dumped body in vineyard’ 600 miles from his home

A DOMESTIC abuser was wearing an electronic monitoring tag when he allegedly murdered a TikTok star 600 miles from his home city, detectives say.

The suspect, 32, was arrested and charged over Sonia Bellina’s violent death in France after police used the ankle tag to track him down.



It comes after the battered and partially burnt body of influencer Sonia, 29, was found in an isolated vineyard close to southern Nimes on August 12.

He faces life in prison for allegedly luring her to the remote area before violently killing her and trying to burn her corpse.



The defendant, who cannot be named for legal reasons, is a known criminal from Lille, in northern France, and was being monitored because of his violence towards a domestic partner.

This meant he was still wearing an ankle tag when he met Sonia on August 10, some 600 miles away from his home city.

The anti-proximity monitor is a GPS-enabled tracking device worn by high-risk offenders to enforce restraining orders.

An investigating source told The Sun: “Detectives used it to trace the alleged killer in the days after Sonia’s death.

“The geographical data is part of the evidence which led to his arrest.”

DNA belonging to the alleged killer was also found on Sonia’s defiled body, and his phone records show he was regularly speaking to Sonia, before meeting her twice.



The Sun previously revealed how Sonia – who was days away from celebrating her 30th birthday – had told family she was going to “end a toxic relationship” hours before she was killed.

It has also emerged that Sonia started working as an escort this year – something that is perfectly legal – and had met her attacker through an online agency.

Cécile Gensac, the Nimes prosecutor who is leading the investigation, confirmed the suspect, who was charged on Friday, was Sonia’s “last contact”.

She said he met her “in the context of an appointment for escort services on the night of the incident”.

Sonia’s lifeless body was discovered by a farm worker on August 12, poorly concealed between two rows of vines in the town of Saint-Gilles.



While in custody, the suspect – who has convictions for domestic abuse an dother violent crimes – has admitted to “having had a relationship with the victim on the night of the incident and the day before”.

He refused, however, to answer any other questions from investigators, said Ms Gensac.

The defendant was brought before an investigating magistrate on Friday afternoon and remanded in custody.



A second man was arrested last week as part of the investigation, but he was cleared of any wrongdoing and released.

One family member has told detectives that Sonia set off in the early hours of the morning “to end a toxic relationship” with an unidentified man.

An investigating source said: “She left without a bag, saying she would be back within a few hours.

“Sonia has only recently met the man, and nobody else in her circle knew him. He was certainly a mystery man.”

The enquiry into Sonia’s death is currently focused on the theory that a man she knew arranged to meet her, before driving her to the place where she was killed.



There was a five-hour window from the moment Sonia left her family apartment in Nimes and the presumed time of death.

“This has been calculated at shortly after her phone being switched off,” the investigating source added.

“Her phone was later found thrown away by the side of the road.”

Sonia was born and brought up in Nimes, where she trained to be a beauty therapist, specialising in eyelash extensions.

Beyond her professional work, she was a hugely popular online influencer, with more than 250,000 followers on TikTok, as well as on other mass audience platforms, such as Instagram and Snapchat.



Her regular performances included lip-synching to old romantic movies, and also pretending to seduce her fans.

Prostitution is legal in France, despite women involved often becoming the victims of a range of crimes, ranging from murder and rape, to other forms of abuse.

A study by French health monitoring organisation Inserm published last November revealed that 80 per cent of women involved in prostitution were subjected to violence, and 70 per cent to forced sexual acts.

Other enquiry sources said Sonia had been spending a lot of time in Paris, which is some 550 miles from her home city of Nimes.

Pictures posted on her social media sites show her in cafés, restaurants and shops identified as being in the French capital.



All of Sonia’s social media accounts have now been deleted.

She did not have any criminal convictions, but had been a victim of assault and theft in the past, enquiry sources confirmed.

Mourad Battikh, the barrister representing the Bellina family, said he was preparing a legal complaint against people who had aimed ‘online insults’ against Sonia’s memory.

Her alleged killer will remain in custody until a murder trial is held later this year.

News.title: Mum, dad and son, 19, plunge to their deaths from cliff as family dispute over mobile phone purchase turns into tragedy
News.content:
DEADLY ROW Mum, dad and son, 19, plunge to their deaths from cliff as family dispute over mobile phone purchase turns into tragedy

A TEENAGER and his parents plunged to their deaths from a cliff after a dispute over an iPhone he bought turned into a tragedy.

Following an argument with his father, Kunal Chandude, 19, made his way to Khavda Hill, India, reportedly with the intention of taking his own life.

For nearly three hours on Friday, his parents begged him to step away from the cliff’s edge as he threatened to jump.



Tragedy struck in the worst way imaginable when Kunal and his parents -dad Murlidhar, 48, and mum Sangita – all plunged from the cliff edge.



Kunal bought an expensive iPhone to be paid off in monthly instalments but was unable to afford it, the Indian Express reports.

A argument erupted between Kunal and his father, who worked as a driver, when the teenager asked for money to pay the latest instalment, which the parents refused.

How to get help EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now. If you, or anyone you know, needs help dealing with mental health problems, the following organisations provide support: CALM, www.thecalmzone.net, 0800 585 858

Heads Together,www.headstogether.org.uk

HUMEN www.wearehumen.org

Mind, www.mind.org.uk, 0300 123 3393

Papyrus, www.papyrus-uk.org, 0800 068 41 41

Samaritans,www.samaritans.org, 116 123

The teenager made his was to the hill in Tisgaon around 10am and his parents followed closely behind.



Hours later around 1pm Murlidhar tried to grab the teen but as he came close Kunal jumped.

Police say his father fell while attempting to save him, other reports suggest he was pulled.

According to the District Collector and Magistrate Vinay Gowda: “The boy fell from the cliff and holding on to his father’s hand, pulled him down with him.”

Sangita watched as her husband and son fell from the edge.



Conflicting reports leave it unclear whether the mother’s fall from the cliff was accidental or intentional.

Police, villagers and firefighters also spent hours trying to bring him down.

Fire personnel attempted to place a safety net below the hill, but Kunal kept moving along the edge of the cliff, officials said.

The police investigation into the tragic incident is underway.

A postmortem has been completed and the bodies have been returned to their relatives.

News.title: BA cabin worker cleared of sexually assaulting colleague after vodka-fuelled wild night out
News.content:
AIR DRAMA BA cabin worker cleared of sexually assaulting colleague after vodka-fuelled wild night out

A BRITISH Airways steward has been cleared of sexually assaulting his female colleague in Rio after staff had a vodka-fuelled wild night out.

A jury of five men and seven women acquitted Ryan Lim, 31, of the offence on Thursday at Isleworth Crown Court.



He had been accused of pleasuring himself while rubbing the stewardess’s bottom as she slept in a hotel bed with him and another male on the morning of November 10, 2024

She claimed she was woken by Lim’s “sexual moaning” before seeing his hand moving up and down in a bedroom mirror.



The crew had gone on a drinking spree after arriving in Rio de Janeiro from London.

The captain bought a bottle of vodka in a club around midnight, the court heard.

At the nightclub, the victim said the BA captain bought a bottle of vodka and was handing out glasses of the spirit to his crew, including Lim and her.

The male colleague whose room she would later sleep in began vomiting, and the alleged victim looked after him.



She had drunk two glasses of vodka with a mixer at the club.

The woman claimed she was about “five-out-of-ten” drunk.

And she said that she does not recall how she ended up sleeping in her male colleague’s room.

His Honour Judge Simon Davis presided over the trial, with Lily Hayes prosecuting and Sophia Kerridge defending.

The alleged assault was reported to Brazilian police and the BA captain.



Two BA flights were cancelled as a result.

Kerridge, defending, said previously: “You woke up in a room with two boys, you were coming in and out of sleep when you noticed something that could be sexual activity.

“At the time you were not sure what you had experienced was something more innocent.

“I suggest to you it didn’t happen because you would have been in a rush to leave that room.”

News.title: Constance Marten granted permission to appeal 14-year jail sentence for killing her baby while on the run with partner
News.content:
APPEAL GRANTED Constance Marten granted permission to appeal 14-year jail sentence for killing her baby while on the run with partner

CONSTANCE Marten has been granted permission to appeal the 14-year jail sentence she was handed for her baby’s death while on the run with her partner.

Marten, 39, and convicted rapist Mark Gordon, 52, were in hiding when their baby daughter, Victoria, died in a tent on the South Downs in southern England in January 2023.



They had fled authorities to prevent Victoria being taken into care, as four other siblings had been before, their Old Bailey trial was told.

Marten and Gordon were found guilty of her manslaughter, child cruelty, concealing the birth of a child and perverting the course of justice following two trials spanning six months each.



Judge Mark Lucraft KC jailed them both for 14 years and handed Gordon a further four years on extended licence.

Marten has now been granted permission to appeal the sentence, and renewed her application for permission to appeal her gross negligence manslaughter conviction.



A court date is yet to be set.

Judge Lucraft accepted the prosecution case that baby Victoria died from hypothermia after being exposed to “significant cold stress”.

He rejected the defendants’ claims that Victoria was smothered in a “terrible accident” as they slept in the tent.

The offending was made worse because the baby was vulnerable and the defendants failed to listen to past warnings.



In a televised sentencing, Judge Lucraft told the defendants: “It is clear throughout the period neither of you gave much or any thought for the care or love for your baby.”

The judge said they had displayed “arrogance” and treated Victoria to “neglect of the most serious type”.

Police had launched a nationwide hunt after the couple’s car burst into flames on a motorway near Bolton, Greater Manchester, on January 5 2023.

The defendants travelled across England and went off-grid, sleeping in a tent on the South Downs where baby Victoria died days later.

After seven weeks on the run, the defendants were arrested in Brighton.



After a desperate search, police found their baby dead amid rubbish inside a Lidl bag in a disused shed nearby.

News.title: Chillingly simple messages reveal how would-be bomber joined ISIS before ‘plotting sick attack on government building’
News.content:
CHILLINGLY simple messages have revealed how a would-be bomber joined ISIS on social media before allegedly planning a sick attack on a government building.

Jessica Bowie, 35, plotted to blow up the New York State Capitol with a bomb hidden in a delivery bag, according to the FBI.



She is accused of pledging allegiance to ISIS and saying “blowing non-Muslims’ brains out is beautiful”.

Terrifying messages show how a terrorist recruiter asked her to take an oath to “obey”, court documents allege.



Prosecutors said Bowie, from Albany, New York, received a message from an unidentified militant on a “well-known” social media site on May 28.

The user allegedly told her in Arabic that she must repeat the words: “We pledge our allegiance to the Commander of the Faithful and the Caliph of the Muslims, the Mujahid Sheikh Abu Hafs al-Hashimi al-Qurashi, to listen and obey.”



She replied: “So, I’m just saying this?”

Her handler replied: “Until you join the [Islamic State].”

Bowie wrote back: “Saying this means joining the [Islamic State]?”

The unidentified militant replied: “Yes.”



She then immediately sent an audio recording of her repeating the words, promising obedience to the leader of ISIS, according to the complaint.

Bowie allegedly sent another audio file with another loyalty oath to a different suspected terrorist on another social media site two days later.

Authorities said the messages showed how Bowie was “radicalised online”.



The New York native allegedly started planning an attack on the Capitol in Albany in July.

Bowie unknowingly hatched the plan alongside FBI informants posing as “ISIS facilitators”, cops said.

FBI agents claimed to have uncovered a plot to place a homemade bomb in a DoorDash food delivery bag outside the building to “kill the senators”.

Bowie, who converted to Islam five years ago and now goes by the Islamic name Aisha Saif, is accused of buying bomb materials from Home Depot.

Shocking footage showed a woman in all black, including gloves and a burqa, appearing to fill up a trolley with bomb parts on August 5.



In other messages, Bowie said she was inspired by a terror plot that killed one and injured 29 others at a pride parade in Berlin.

She allegedly wrote: “You look at this brother in, what is it? Germany? He did a great thing, but only one person died. When he rammed into the crowd of the people.

Bowie told an informant that she had been a little girl “waving the American flag” following 9/11 to owning stickers celebrating the fallen towers, according to the FBI.



She was kicked off one social media platform for writing: “Praise be to Allah for September 11th,” police said.

Bowie was arrested on Wednesday after agents handed her a fake gun and fake detonator, the FBI said.

She allegedly planned to flee to Syria after the planned attack.

Bowie offered a partial confession during her interview with FBI agents, according to the complaint.

The woman allegedly said: “There’s no helping me, you guys know enough, there’s no helping me, I’m going to prison for the rest of my life.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Material support is up to 20 years in prison, I already Googled it before, I know I’m going to jail.”

FBI Special Agent in Charge Albany Field Office Craig L. Tremaroli said after the arrest: “Ms. Bowie didn’t just want to kill lawmakers; she wanted a complete destruction of our government.”

News.title: Missing grandma Alisa Goods’ harrowing last moments revealed in surveillance video after cops find body in ditch
News.content:
TRAGIC DISCOVERY Missing grandma Alisa Goods’ harrowing last moments revealed in surveillance video after cops find body in ditch

THE final moments of missing grandma Alisa Goods’ life have been revealed by surveillance footage after cops found her body in a ditch.

The 63-year-old from New York was found dead near Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas on Thursday.



She had been missing for two weeks after leaving the house of a longtime friend to go shopping.

Now cops have revealed more details about the mom-of-five’s final moments after fears were raised about foul play, after haunting texts were sent from her phone.



In a statement to The U.S. Sun, the LVMPD confirmed that they were called to a drainage ditch near the airport’s Terminal 1 parking garage on August 20 at around 1:45am.

“Officers arrived and located the female who was confirmed to be deceased.

“Subsequent review of video surveillance from the airport shows the woman falling down an embankment, getting back up and then collapsing on August 8, 2026.

“There was no further movement observed after that. Her location could not be seen from the street.”

She was soon identified as Alisa Goods but no official cause of death has been released.

Her family revealed to KTNV that she had recently had several surgeries on her legs, though it is unclear if this is related to her death.



“Our hearts are broken. We were notified that my aunt was found — unfortunately, not the way we wanted her to be,” Goods’ niece, Alana Calloway, said in a statement.

“This is an unimaginable time. Words cannot describe the pain our family is experiencing right now.

“We just want to thank the public for the outpouring of love, support, and prayers…This hurts so deeply. We are still trying to learn the details surrounding her death.

“We ask for continued prayers and privacy as we grieve.”

Goods had been staying with pal Roger John, as she regularly did when visiting Sin City.



On August 8, she left the apartment around 12:45pm to go to a local CVS store but never returned.

Days later, her family said someone began responding from her phone and asking for money which raised fears of foul play.

However, Las Vegas cops told The U.S. Sun they had dismissed whoever was using her phone, stressing they were just “bad actors” and not connected to her status as a missing person.

News.title: Drink-driver, 40, who killed schoolgirl, 13, in horror car crash told teen passengers trying to save her to lie to cops
News.content:
KILLER CAGED Drink-driver, 40, who killed schoolgirl, 13, in horror car crash told teen passengers trying to save her to lie to cops

A DRUNK-DRIVER who killed a 13-year-old girl in the passenger seat told other teens in the car to lie to the police.

Dwane Moody, 40, was uninsured and unlicensed and had been drinking alcohol at a party when he drove three teens in an another guest’s car on January 31.



He left the event in Hertfordshire on New Year’s Eve and was seen driving erratically and at speed.

Moody eventually failed to navigate a corner and the car went through a fence, seriously injuring Evelyn, who was in the front seat.



While the two other teens called 999 and began administering first aid, Moody demanded they lie to the operators.

He asked them to say a vehicle coming the other way had forced them off the road, threatening them to give a false account.



Emergency services arrived and Moody was arrested before being taken to a hospital and then custody.

All three teenagers were taken to hospital, where Evelyn tragically died four days later.

On Friday, Moody, of Dane End, appeared at St Albans Crown Court and was sentenced to 12 years and 8 months in prison.

He had pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to causing death by dangerous driving, causing death whilst uninsured, and causing death whilst otherwise in accordance with a licence.



Moody also pleaded guilty to two counts of perverting the course of justice and aggravated taking (of a vehicle) without consent.

In addition to the custodial sentence, he has been banned from driving for 17 years and four months.

The young girl’s parents have released moving tributes to their daughter following Moody’s arrest.

Evelyn’s mother said: “She was a child who absolutely loved life. She brought an infectious energy into our home, and her presence was pure light.

“One of her absolute favourite places to be was on her trampoline. I can still close my eyes and see her jumping, laughing and defying gravity, just bursting with youth and happiness.



“She had so much life left to live, so many more days to jump, play and grow. The defendant didn’t just cause a crash; he shattered my entire universe.”

Evelyn’s father said: “Evelyn was the light of all our worlds, there wasn’t a day that would go by without her making us laugh or smile.

“Our family is a chain, and she was the strongest link keeping us all together and now that link is no longer there, but we are still holding on strong, never losing her name and keeping her in our hearts.”

Det Con Lewis Stanley, from the serious collision investigation unit, said: “This is a tragic case in which a young girl lost her life unnecessarily.

“Evelyn’s family have shown immense strength throughout this investigation and our thoughts remain with them as they continue to come to terms with their devastating loss.



“Dwane Moody made a series of reckless and selfish decisions that evening.

“It speaks volumes of his character that he, a grown man, was trying to persuade the other passengers, both teenagers, to lie for him whilst they were trying to save Evelyn.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They suffered a hugely traumatic ordeal and I would like to commend them for their brave actions.

“No sentence can undo the pain caused by Evelyn’s death.”

News.title: Dramatic moment cops smash down doors of £15m Thundercrest drug ring flooding UK with heroin & ket hidden with kids’ toy
News.content:
AT DAWN the sound of smashed glass tinkling onto the pavement can barely be heard through the driving rain.

Cops carefully lay down a Kevlar rug and silently start climbing through the shattered window and into the house.



With an almighty roar, sudden shouts of “police, stay where you are” announce the officers’ arrival to the oblivious residents and their sleeping neighbours.

Unbeknown to his family, the dazed young man being put in cuffs is suspected of being a key player in a serious organised crime group couriering kilos of Class A drugs to other gangs nearly 300 miles away.



But now they’ve been taken out of play.



His arrest is one of the 12 warrants being executed in tightly coordinated 6am raids.

The gang is suspected of having trafficked 200kgs of drugs – potentially netting £15million in profits.

Five minutes away a simultaneous raid is taking place. As law enforcement are outside sawing the door in half, the baffled suspect opens it.



It’s a rude awakening for his younger family members who have no idea he’s allegedly involved in couriering drugs to Plymouth, Glasgow, Gloucester and Swansea as well as London.

The morning of action on Wednesday saw nine people aged between 20 and 56, including one woman, arrested for conspiracy to supply Class A drugs.

Greater Manchester Police spent nearly a year working on their case to take down the alleged gang in Operation Adela.

Detective Sergeant Richard McCorry said: “This was a very well-embedded and sophisticated organised crime group that has likely been running for a few years.”



DS McCorry’s team is planning more arrests to pick up the final members of the gang hiding in Manchester.

He warns them: “We’re watching you. This isn’t the end.”

Over the course of their investigation cops have seized 36kgs of drugs -primarily cocaine and heroin – but they’ve also taken ketamine and cannabis, alongside a variety of Class C drugs.



Nationwide, cocaine seizures are up 13 per cent year on year, with powder cocaine accounting for 60 per cent of all drugs found, according to Government figures.

Between March 2024 and March 2025, more than 18 tonnes of cocaine was found by cops and Border Force.

Back in the house with the smashed bay window, officers find two kilograms of cocaine – the same amount they found on a suspected courier for the gang at the weekend en route to Gloucester.

Then, in a storage unit police raided, a further four kilograms of cocaine was discovered hidden among kids’ clothing and toys.

It was just a few hundred yards from a primary school.



Also stashed inside the unit was £2,000 made up of bundles of £50 notes in a safe, plus a cash counting machine.

Detective sergeant Rob O’Brien said: “Drugs is a cash rich business.

“They won’t want to spend time rummaging. They want to be in and out as quickly as possible.”



Police dog Bruce was also brought in to search the rest of the shipping container to make sure no other drugs were hidden away.

Five men and one woman have been charged with conspiracy to supply Class A drugs namely cocaine and heroin.

Another man has been charged with possession with intent to supply Class A drugs, and a final man with conspiracy to money launder and participate in the activities of an Organised Crime Group.



For Greater Manchester Police, their war on drugs is far from over as they’re determined to stamp out the criminals peddling narcotics at home and away.

At 5.40am on Thursday morning, four flats in a newbuild block in Swinton, Salford, were raided with doors sawed in half before being smashed in.

As one of the doors gave way, a black and tan sausage dog shot out and scurried away from the noise. The terrified pup was later found by GMP’s drone squad and brought home.



Alerted to the cops by the screams of the reciprocating saw, one man attempted to flee by climbing out a first floor bathroom window in nothing but his tracksuit bottoms.

His escape bid failed, and he was cuffed by waiting officers.

The four flats are suspected of being linked by a drugs line which is being investigated as part of Operation Thundercrest.



It’s flooding the area with Class A drugs crack cocaine and heroin.

And officers believe that there is modern slavery and possible “cuckooing” – a sinister tactic in which dealers use violence, drugs and manipulation to take over a vulnerable person’s home.

These suspects were arrested in new-build council-run temporary housing for those who have been homeless. Each flat comes with an electric car charging point, but there isn’t a single car in the drive.

No charges have been brought yet in relation to the Salford warrants.

Neighbourhood Chief Inspector Lee Gridley, for GMP’s Salford District, told The Sun: “This line has been running for a few months and drugs bring with them all kinds of criminality.



“Theft of motor vehicles, burglaries. Today we’ve recovered distinctive property that we believe is from a local recent burglary.

“We’ve got to work out the levels of criminality for the men arrested today.

“Vulnerable people are preyed upon by others. That isn’t lost on us and we will be looking closely at this.



“A line has been disrupted preventing harmful drugs from reaching the streets and vulnerable people being exploited.”

Six men were arrested in the Thursday raids on a variety of charges including possession with intent to supply, possession of an offensive weapon and burglary.

Across the UK, the amount of heroin seized has increased by 33 per cent since 2024 – with police and Border Force finding 589kgs compared to 441kgs between March 2023 and 2024.

Crack cocaine seizures have also gone up by 106 per cent from 40kgs to 81kgs, compared to the previous year.

Often gangs will use addiction to coerce people into criminality and the affects of addiction can be devastating as Tony, a Forward Trust lived experience ambassador, knows.



“I was consumed by my addiction,” he said.

“Every minute of every day was an endless cycle of trying to get money to use and then using.

“I think people think that using drugs like crack is enjoyable. The truth is it really isn’t. You use crack to get high.

“Once you’re high you feel like you need to come down so you use heroin. At no point do you ever feel content. Just this feeling that the next one will solve the problem but it never does.”

He added: “I started using drugs at 11 and heroin and crack at 15. For years I was in and out of addiction, prison and homelessness. I lost my kids, relationships and pretty much everything that mattered to me.



“I’ve spent about 15 years of my life in prison because of the lifestyle that came with my addiction. I’m nearly 5 years clean now which is mad when I think about where I came from.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And it’s to protect communities and people like Tony that cops keep on working to take out drug lines.

“You should be afraid,” CI Gridley warned the organised crime gangs. “We’re always watching.”

News.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
News.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

News.title: As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks
News.content:
In late July, the Duchess of Sussex's lifestyle range, called As ever, launched a "rich, vibrant" blackberry spread alongside a softly lit video of her picking the fruit.

A month later, Meghan and her husband Prince Harry are returning to live in the UK just as blackberry season ends. Perhaps we can expect another video soon, shot on these shores.

Or perhaps not, because experts say the Harry and Meghan brand is at a crossroads.

After the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's acrimonious exit from the Royal Family in 2020, the projects marking their fresh start in California - from streaming to signature scents - have mostly failed to find large audiences, and experts say it's unclear where the couple goes from here.

Their return to the UK has surprised many and we don't know their reasons for the switch, but what's clear is that they will not be working royals when they return. So what could they be doing instead?

News.title: Watch: Moment robot attempts to beat Usain Bolt's 100m record
News.content:
A humanoid robot has outperformed humans by breaking Usain Bolt's world record for the 100m sprint, according to its manufacturer.

Chinese smartphone maker Honor said Lightning - a thin black and red robot - ran the distance in 9.32 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing.

Eight-time Olympic gold medallist Bolt set the world record for humans in 2009, running 100m in 9.58 seconds.

Other events at the robot games, which started on Saturday, include boxing and football, but also household tasks like folding laundry.

More than 2,000 robots from 16 countries are expected to compete in the games. The event comes as China showcases its heavy investment in robotics.

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

News.title: These bookshops let Chinese readers question their country, now the doors are closing
News.content:
When Chen Zhu heads to Hong Kong from mainland China every month, there's one place she always goes: Hunter Bookstore.

Founded four years ago by a former councillor, the independent bookshop has earned a reputation for stocking what authorities would consider sensitive books - from accounts of Hong Kong's pro-democracy campaigners, to famous allegories on authoritarianism, such as George Orwell's Animal Farm or Hajime Isayama's Manga series Attack on Titan.

It's a short journey from Zhu's home in Guangzhou on China's southern coast to the crowded street in Hong Kong's Sham Shui Po district, where Hunter is sandwiched between fabric sellers, garages and trendy cafes.

But, for the 23-year-old, it is also a passage into a different, freer world - where she can find answers to forbidden questions.

When she learned the bookshop had been raided by police in late June, Zhu broke into tears: "I was devastated."

Hong Kong saw a boom in independent bookshops after huge pro-democracy protests rocked the city in 2019. But it has been increasingly difficult for them to survive as China's control over the city has grown.

While Beijing defends its far-reaching National Security Law (NSL) as essential for stability, many Hong Kongers and rights groups argue it has crushed free speech. Thousands of locals, including activists and former lawmakers, have left in recent years, as tough new security laws have led to a slew of arrests and convictions.

News.title: Two-time world boxing champion Tete shot dead outside home
News.content:
Two-time world champion Zolani Tete has been shot dead outside his home in South Africa.

The 38âyearâold was killed in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape on Friday.

Officials said Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27âyearâold female passenger, who remains in hospital.

South Africa's minister of sport, arts and culture, Gayton McKenzie, said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

The two suspects fled the scene and a major investigation has been launched, McKenzie added.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014.

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a four-year ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

His ban ended on 29 July, 2026 and after his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

News.title: Girl, 6, dies after family killed in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident which also killed her father, mother and sister.

Saja El-Khawas, a British Palestinian from London, was pulled from the sea by emergency crews on Tuesday.

Her father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old sister Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene.

Emergency services were called to the sea off Shoreham Fort at about 14:40 BST on Tuesday to a report of four people in difficulty in the water.

News.title: Advisor O'Neill rules out government job but backs PM's devolution plans
News.content:
The economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer, was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, he said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had "lots of other things that are going on that I very much enjoy" and, having been a minister before, he knew the job included "all the constraints that understandably go with it, like a blind trust and to abandon everything else you do, never mind the fact that it's 24/7".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

He said he concluded he would rather be a voice to talk to and "get on with the rest of the things in my life".

He earlier told the Financial Times it was "not because of any policy disagreements", adding "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

He pointed to Greater Manchester as an example of economic growth and said if you could repeat that around populated areas, "then national economic performance will improve".

Asked by the BBC whether the new government in the upcoming October budget would need to raise taxes, Lord O'Neill said it was a choice for the prime minister and his team "based on the things they're saying they want to do more of - defence spending is obviously the one that catches the eye", among other things.

Pressed on whether the government could turn to something such as wealth taxes, Lord O'Neill said he was "not a fan of further increases in these kind of taxes, particularly as it relates to capital gains for genuine risk taking things like venture capital".

He noted that the country has boosted government spending "dramatically" in recent years and needed a "more sensible approach to welfare spending under genuine welfare reform".

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

News.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

News.title: Murder probe after wildfire uncovers body in park
News.content:
A murder investigation is under way after human bones were uncovered at a west London park following a wildfire, the Metropolitan Police said.

Emergency services were called to Bedfont Pits in Hounslow at about 18:35 BST on Wednesday, 12 August.

A police spokesperson said the remains were found by a member of the public after the wildfire affected an area of woodland known as The Pits.

Following a post-mortem examination, police said the bones belonged to a woman aged between 25 and 45. They said it was not clear how long the remains had been there and officers were still working to identify her.

News.title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' by passenger rescued from sea
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has been arrested after a ferry service on Scotland's west coast was evacuated over a bomb threat.

Operator CalMac said a passenger was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 service, carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.

The BBC understands that after being pulled from the sea by the ferry's rescue boat, the man then told crew that there was a bomb on board.

All passengers were removed on foot at Ardrossan so the vessel could be searched. Police Scotland said it was established that the threats "were not credible".

The passengers and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby supermarket car park by police while the search was carried out.

After this was complete, officers allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.

News.title: Teen blinded by firework wants ban on public sales
News.content:
A teenager blinded by a firework on Bonfire Night has called for a ban on them being sold to the public.

Tom Parnaby was 18 when he and a friend were badly injured in the accident on 5 November 2025.

He is now campaigning for more controlled firework displays and tighter regulations on sales.

Tom, who has since become a father for the first time, said despite what happened to him he does not hate fireworks, but thinks the "public sale of them is crazy".

Tom suffered injuries to his face leading to him losing his sight during an incident with friends on the beach in Scarborough, North Yorkshire.

The teenager said focusing on the baby daughter who he would never be able to see had helped him pull through.

"I am just grateful to have her with me," he said.

"It is a lot easier to focus on what's coming than what's behind with her there."

News.title: Man tracks down siblings who sent him Christmas present as he fled war 33 years ago
News.content:
A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more than 30 years ago.

Dalibor Sentic was 10 when in the early 1990s his family fled the newly independent country - which had recently become involved in the Balkan war - for Stockholm, Sweden.

Dalibor had received a gift from two young siblings, eight-year-old Claire and Peter, six, from Mold, Flintshire, and had hoped to track them down but only had limited information on them.

Decades later, Dalibor, now 44, was able to find the pair to thank them, saying the gesture had "meant a lot" at a time of great difficulty.

Describing fleeing his homeland as a child, Dalibor said "we had basically nothing".

"It was like starting all over again.

"I was so innocent but remember hearing the bombs," he said.

Dalibor said that, despite the conflict surrounding them, his parents made sure he felt "loved and secure", although he added that moving countries was "tough on a kid".

Some months before they fled, Dalibor said his teacher took him into a room full of packages, telling him to choose one to open.

It contained a picture of Claire and Peter, which he held onto for more than three decades.

"The older you get the more you understand the meaning behind small gestures... it meant a lot," he said.

Seven people have died, including two police officers, after a VW travelling in the wrong direction crashed into a police vehicle following a chase.

Fourteen ambulance crews were sent to the devastating incident involving two serving officers in a marked police car and five members of the public in a Volkswagen Passat.

The Passat was travelling the wrong way along the A66 and collided with a police vehicle that was travelling in the right direction at about 3.39am in South Bank, near Middlesborough in Teesside, Cleveland Police said.

Sadly, all occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene.

The police watchdog the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) confirmed it has launched an investigation into the fatal crash.

Officers from Cleveland Police spotted a suspicious vehicle and a pursuit began before the car travelled onto the A66 and collided with a police car, the watchdog said.

open image in gallery Police officers at the scene of a fatal crash involving a police car and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough ( Owen Humphreys/PA )

IOPC director of investigations Nicola Marfleet said: “This is a tragic incident, and my thoughts are with family and friends and all those affected, including the emergency services in attendance.

“Our investigation is in the very early stages, we have sent investigators to the post incident procedures to begin reviewing evidence.

“When someone dies following police contact, it is mandatory that the matter is referred to the IOPC. Our role is to establish and examine the circumstances of what happened; this work is already underway, and Cleveland Police is cooperating with our enquiries.”

Officers are still working to formally identify all the occupants of the Passat.

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood said the tragedy was “devastating”.

“Police officers put their own safety on the line to protect their communities every single day,” she added. “The two officers were on active duty, serving the people of Cleveland.

“My thoughts are with all those affected, their families, friends, the emergency services who attended the scene and the wider police family.”

open image in gallery A police cordon at the scene of a fatal crash on the A66 in South Bank ( Owen Humphreys/PA )

Anna Turley, MP for the Redcar constituency where the crash happened, said she was “deeply saddened” and warned people against speculating online.

“Cleveland Police have confirmed that seven people have sadly lost their lives,” she added. “Their families and loved ones are now facing an unimaginable loss that will be felt forever.

“Two of the seven people who have lost their lives were Cleveland Police officers, on duty serving our community. They went to work to keep people safe and they should have come home to their families.

“Their loss will be felt deeply by their loved ones, fellow officers and right across the communities they served.”

The MP thanked emergency services for their “courage, care and professionalism” responding to the shocking crash, adding: “Cleveland Police are investigating the accident, alongside the Independent Office for Police Conduct. It is crucial that we respect that process and avoid speculation at this deeply painful time.”

open image in gallery The police watchdog has launched an investigation into the fatal crash ( PA )

The road is closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane.

The closed section of the A66 is bordered by large industrial units to the north, and is close to the major Teesworks site.

There is significant emergency response at the scene and people should use alternative routes as the road “will remain closed for some time”, Cleveland Police said.

Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said: “First and foremost, our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in today’s incident.

“No one should leave their home and not return safely, including police officers serving their communities and protecting the people of Cleveland.

“This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family. We are providing specialist support to all families involved at this extremely difficult time.

“The investigation has been referred to the IOPC, which is the standard approach when a death occurs following police contact. We will cooperate fully with their investigation.

“While this investigation takes place, we strongly urge people to avoid speculation."

open image in gallery A large police cordon is in place ( PA )

The chairwoman of Cleveland Police Federation, Lauren Somerville, said “words cannot describe the pain” of losing two officers.

“Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable,” she said.

David Taylor and Stephen Martin, councillors for the Eston ward, said they were “deeply saddened” by the “unimaginable tragedy”.

A post on their Facebook page read: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating news that seven people have lost their lives following a collision on the A66 at South Bank in the early hours of this morning.”

It continued: “This is an unimaginable tragedy that will be felt deeply throughout TS6 and communities across Cleveland and around the country. Absolutely heartbreaking.”

A North East Ambulance Service spokesman said they sent 14 ambulances resources to the scene, including emergency ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic, our Hazardous Area Response Team and a doctor from Great North Air Ambulance Service.

“Sadly despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene,” the spokesman added. “We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help.”

More follows on this breaking news story....

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to retaliate after a double-tap drone strike on his home town killed 16 people.

Rescuers are still searching for survivors in the wreckage of a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, that was hit twice by Russia on Friday.

More than 130 people were wounded in a daytime attack carried out in two waves, with the second strike targeting emergency workers at the scene of the first.

Zelensky called the attacks an “act of barbarism”, claiming the “absolutely cynical and despicable” second strike was a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.

open image in gallery Firefighters work on a fire at a shopping mall following a Russian drone attack in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine ( AP )

“Attacks like these are nothing less than ⁠terrorist acts,” Zelensky said on Telegram, urging the world to hold Russia to account. “We will definitely respond.”

Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that 22 children were among the wounded and nine people including two children were missing.

“There are 29 people ​in ⁠serious condition, including five children,” Hanzha said adding that rescuers were continuing to clear the rubble of the shopping centre.

Rescue teams from four other Ukrainian regions have been deployed to help search for survivors.

open image in gallery The mall was hit twice, with the second strike coming half an hour after the first as emergency workers were on the scene ( Telegram/Prosecutor General's Office )

Kryvyi Rih Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the Russian drones were flying at “extremely low altitudes”, describing the attackers as “animals”.

“There are missing people who are not responding to calls,” the mayor added.

Zelensky renewed his calls for more air defence support following the strikes. In a post on X he said: “Every day that Ukraine lacks sufficient air defence means casualties that could have been prevented.

”Protecting lives requires daily decisions and effective support from the world, and right now, new supplies of ballistic missile interceptors and other missiles can help.”

European Commission vice president Kaja Kallas has called the attack “terror by design”.

She said in a post on X that the strike shows the “absolute and utter depravity of Moscow's war”.

open image in gallery Rescuers work at the site of a shopping centre destroyed by Friday's drone attack by Russia ( Reuters )

“Russia wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable,” she added. “I am putting forward the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war. The pressure must be intensified until Moscow ends the war.”

Kryvyi Rih in particular has been hit multiple times during the war. One of the deadliest occurred in April 2025, when 20 people, including nine children, were killed.

She said EU foreign and defence ministers will discuss how to expand support for Ukraine, including air and missile defence, when they meet in less than two weeks in Dublin.

The attack is the latest in a series of high death toll strikes over the summer.

open image in gallery The attack is the latest in a series of deadly strikes over the summer ( Reuters )

Friday’s attacks landed just 24 hours after Russia hit Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that also killed 16 people.

The capital has been hit hard repeatedly in recent weeks: 17 people were killed in a strike on Kyiv and its surrounding region just over two weeks ago, and nine died in another attack on the city two days before that. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 injured.

At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across the country.

It also has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.

The Russian online news outlet Astra reported Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil refinery in the Samara region. Local officials said damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility” and a logistics center for Ozon, a competitor to Wildberries.

News.title: Two men arrested over young soldier’s mysterious death in River Tyne
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Two men have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after the death of a young soldier who disappeared on a night out with friends.

The two men, aged 22 and 23, were taken into police custody on Saturday.

It came four days after the body of Liam Potts, 22, was found in the River Tyne.

Mr Potts served with the Coldstream Guards, a regiment with a history stretching back to 1650.

He had gone missing following a night out and was last seen heading towards Wylam, in Northumberland, around 12.20am on 15 August.

His body was found a short distance away from Wylam Bridge.

open image in gallery The Coldstream Guards parade during the state opening of Parliament in London on 13 May ( AFP/Getty )

Prior to his disappearance, Northumbria Police had received a report of a disturbance and subsequent collision involving a vehicle and a group of pedestrians on the bridge.

On Monday, police said that two men had been arrested and then bailed in connection with the report.

On Saturday, police said that the men had been re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter.

Detectives were investigating whether the disturbance and collision led to Mr Potts entering the water, they said.

Mr Potts was not in the vehicle involved in the collision, nor was he struck by it, police said.

When Mr Potts’s body was found, police did not believe there to be any third-party involvement. However, further inquiries had prompted the re-arrest of the men, police added.

A man and a woman, both in their 20s, suffered serious injuries in the collision.

The woman has since been been discharged from hospital, while the man remains in hospital for further treatment.

No formal identification of the body pulled from the River Tyne has taken place, but Mr Potts’s next-of-kin have been informed.

His family said he was the “heart of soul of any room”.

In a tribute addressed to “our Liam”, they said: “You may no longer be here beside us, but your presence will never be forgotten. Your family, friends and colleagues have all said the same thing, ‘once you met Pottsy, you could never forget him.’

“We are going to miss your smile, your laugh and the little things that made you who you are. Though time may pass, the love we have for you will never fade.

“You will always be remembered, and forever loved. Rest peacefully, knowing that your memory lives on in all those whose lives you touched.”

Senior investigating officer Detective Inspector Rachael Rutherford, of Northumbria Police, said: “Our thoughts remain with Liam’s family during this difficult time.

“The facts remain the same that Liam was on the bridge at the time of the collision, but he was not an occupant of the vehicle and was not struck by the vehicle.

“Inquiries have revealed that Liam, for reasons yet to be established, entered the water within minutes of the collision.

“We have therefore made the further re-arrests as we are looking to establish whether there is any link between the collision and Liam entering the water.”

Det Insp Rutherford added: “We know there has been a lot of confusion and speculation in the community. It’s clear that Liam was a very popular young man.

“We are committed to finding answers for Liam’s family and we will continue to provide updates on our investigation.

“We would remind people to avoid speculation both online and in our communities as this could impact the ongoing investigation.

“We would continue to ask that people respect the family’s privacy at this tragic time.”

Rather than planting additional flowers, President Donald Trump has filled the White House Rose Garden with sculptures.

Sculptures depicting key American founding figures now sit in the space adjoining the Oval Office.

This follows Trump's decision to substitute the traditional grass lawn with a paved white stone terrace, creating an aesthetic reminiscent of his private Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida.

One featured artwork was donated outright, while several others were provided on temporary loan by undisclosed contributors.

The most recent installation is a bronze sculpture of a seated Thomas Jefferson drafting the Declaration of Independence, crafted and presented by Colorado-based sculptor George Lundeen.

The piece stands alongside depictions of George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, and Ben Franklin, along with a fifth work entitled "Freedom’s Charge."

These installations are part of an extensive program of White House alterations overseen by Trump, including a gilded redesign of the Oval Office and a new ballroom and landing pad being constructed on the southern lawn.

The Republican president's alterations reflect his desire to reshape the capital's architectural landscape, which also includes plans for a monument park on federal grounds near the National Mall.

Lundeen originally produced the artwork representing Jefferson, the third U.S. president, several decades prior, retaining it at his property before deciding to refurbish it and send it to Trump for display at the executive mansion ahead of the Independence Day festivities marking the country's semiquincentennial.

His associate, Steven Barber, initiated communication with administration officials on Lundeen's behalf.

"I thought it would just be a real nice thing on the 250th for people to look at Thomas Jefferson as he was writing the Declaration of Independence," Lundeen said in a telephone interview.

Deliveries were delayed, however, so the piece failed to arrive before the holiday.

open image in gallery Trump Rose Garden Statues ( Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

According to Barber, transport vehicles faced holds amid strict event security protocols. After reviewing photographs of the work, Trump was sufficiently impressed to select a location for it within the Rose Garden.

Direct contact was missed when the president placed an appreciative telephone call that went straight to Lundeen's answering system. Following the holiday period, an office administrator urged Lundeen to review a specific recording.

"Hi, George. It's your favorite president, Donald Trump, and I just wanted to thank you," the president said on the recording, which Lundeen shared with The Associated Press.

"The sculpture, it looks really beautiful ... just by the picture I can see it's really incredible, and we have a wonderful place right in the Rose Garden, and I appreciate it."

Barber said in a separate telephone interview that early attempts to engage White House staff had yielded minimal traction over several months. That changed rapidly roughly three weeks prior to July 4, when officials sent a "flurry of emails saying they wanted it."

Limited background information has been made available regarding the remaining sculptures situated in the patio area.

The White House said Harlan Crow supplied the portrayal of Washington, America's first president, on loan. Representatives for the Texas real estate developer and GOP megadonor, noted for his personal ties to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, did not respond to email messages seeking comment.

Meanwhile, "Freedom's Charge," a 14-foot-tall (4.3-meter-tall) bronze artwork representing two Revolutionary War soldiers flanking a flag, was moved from Dallas. Artist Chas Fagan did not respond to written requests seeking comment.

According to executive staff, the pieces representing Franklin and Hamilton were supplied by unidentified donors.

Addressing the installations, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle asserted that no chief executive in history has committed as much effort toward enhancing the grounds and structure of the residence.

"From restoring our treasured landmarks, which had suffered years of abuse and vandalism, to cleaning our parks and the Reflecting Pool, President Trump’s bold vision ensured that America rang in its 250th birthday celebration with glory and pride," Ingle said in an emailed statement referencing recent maintenance efforts surrounding the Lincoln Memorial pool.

Ingle added that Trump remains committed to delivering "long-overdue and necessary" structural and aesthetic updates throughout the estate.

open image in gallery Trump Rose Garden Statues ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

"Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, the White House will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come," Ingle said.

On the adjacent property of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, Trump oversaw the placement of a Christopher Columbus monument during March.

Additionally, the National Park Service recently erected a collection of works depicting figures and themes from the Revolutionary era at a nearby public plaza.

Trump's most ambitious monument initiative centers on establishing a National Garden of American Heroes close to the National Mall, intended to house statues of 250 historic American figures who made significant cultural, political and historical contributions. However, the proposal faces legal challenges from multiple historic preservation groups, who contend that explicit congressional approval is legally required before work can proceed.

Barber indicated that he and Lundeen remain "in the mix" to contribute sculptures for that proposed memorial grounds as well.

At his private golf facility in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump displays a 7-foot (2.1-meter) bronze piece capturing his raised-fist posture following the 2024 assassination attempt at a Butler, Pennsylvania campaign rally. Created by Lundeen, the sculpture was presented as a gift by Anthony Constantino, a New York entrepreneur and Republican congressional candidate.

The White House has historically served as a showcase for notable artistic works, most famously Gilbert Stuart's portrait of Washington in the East Room—rescued by first lady Dolly Madison during the 1814 burning of the building by British forces during the War of 1812.

open image in gallery Trump Rose Garden Statues ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Sitting presidents hold access to an extensive collection of historic art. Trump noted that he personally examined the "vaults" to select presidential portraits and decorative pieces for display across the Oval Office and executive rooms. Likenesses of former presidents and former first ladies routinely line the public halls and reception rooms.

During Trump's initial term, first lady Melania Trump arranged the placement of a work by Japanese American artist Isamu Noguchi near the Rose Garden, marking the first inclusion of an Asian American artist in the White House collection.

Previously, a 2015 redecoration of the Old Family Dining Room led by then-first lady Michelle Obama introduced a painting by Alma Thomas, who became the first African American female artist represented in the national executive collection.

Hull City fans had a message for Joe Cole as they got their Premier League campaign underway at home with a 2-0 victory over Manchester United.

The club returned to the top flight on Saturday for the first time since 2017 but found themselves on the receiving end of disparaging remarks from Cole on The Dressing Room podcast, where he said he had turned down an offer to work as a TNT Sports pundit at the game as he would be “stunned if they stayed up”.

open image in gallery Joe Cole had made dismissive remarks about Hull's survival chances ( Getty )

In the 38th minute the Tigers’ Nobel Mendy scored their second goal against United, inspiring an ‘Are you watching, Joe Cole?’ chant to echo through the MKM stadium, which was then repeated as the game drew to a close.

The club had their own joke at Cole’s expense after he referenced their play-off win with the claim: “They’ve come here through the back door, they’ve slipped in.”

Marking Saturday’s result, Hull posted on X: “Came through the back door. Left with three points.”

Hull owner Acun Ilicali addressed the remarks in his pre-match interview on TNT, saying: “I was fed up last season, (people tipping us for) relegation – but not like this year.

“This year, everybody’s making predictions. When it comes to Hull, they don’t even talk, just put ‘Hull, 20’ then go straight to the next team.

“That’s what we like, I like, our fans like, because we want to be underdogs. If nobody thinks we will achieve something, I like it like this.

“When we came, they said it was impossible. One agent, I will never forget this, I said ‘We will fight for promotion’. The agent said to me, ‘How can you think of promotion? It’s impossible for you to get promoted. I want my player to go to the Premier League’.

“Of course I ended the conversation immediately and let the player go. But we are coming from these times, so I cannot explain to you how happy I am now to see this beautiful atmosphere. We are playing Manchester United, the fans are here, they are so happy.”

Damon Sacco had never encountered anything resembling the giant fish he and fellow anglers fought for hours in waters off Massachusetts.

As it rose from the sea, it looked like a shimmering blue spaceship.

Sacco, a longtime Massachusetts charter fishing boat captain, spotted the massive fin breaking the water's surface, and at first he believed he was dealing with an enormous shark.

"Then I got a better look at it and thought, dang, that thing's pointed," he said. "But that's too big for a marlin."

He was wrong.

Sacco and his client Walter Chapman landed what they and others believe is the largest Atlantic blue marlin ever taken off the U.S. East Coast on Wednesday.

The massive billfish, more than 11 feet (335 cm) in length, weighed 1,260 pounds (571.5 kilograms) when brought back to land in Falmouth, Massachusetts.

That figure was just 142 pounds (64.4 kilograms) short of the world record for an Atlantic blue marlin, caught off Brazil in 1992, according to records kept by the International Game Fish Association.

Catching such a giant fish off New England is even more remarkable, said Walt Golet, director of the University of Maine Pelagic Fisheries Lab and an associate professor at the university's marine sciences school.

( Katie Curran via AP )

Water temperatures are too cold in the Northeast for most of the year, making the window to land a large one extremely narrow.

The fish’s head was sent to the UMaine laboratory to determine its age, with Golet speculating that it could fall within the range of 25 to 30 years old.

"I don’t suspect there will be a whole lot of blue marlin caught in the Atlantic in general that are going to top 1,200 pounds for the next several years," he said.

On the day of the catch, Sacco's charter boat, Castafari, was fishing Atlantis Canyon, an underwater feature along the edge of the continental shelf about 100 miles (160 kilometers) off Cape Cod. The highly migratory blue marlin is merely a seasonal visitor to the area, Golet said.

The fight against the marlin lasted about three hours and was fought using a rod and reel by Chapman. Sacco said his role for most of the adventure was to "drive the bus around and yell at people." He added that the fish left a couple of holes in the boat's transom with its bill that he considers "war marks."

Chapman, a retiree and lifelong fisherman from Plymouth, said the fish's meat was divided among roughly a dozen people, and he is currently looking up recipes for what to do with it. He noted the marlin is unquestionably the biggest fish he has ever fought on a line, and some of it is likely destined for fish chowder.

"I wasn't going to eat a 1,200 pound fish all by myself," Chapman said.

When the boat returned to the docks, a crowd was waiting, and weighing the fish became a brief spectacle. Onlooker Katie Curran of Falmouth described the sight as truly spectacular.

"People fish their entire lives and never come close to a catch like this," Curran said. "Hats off to Captain Damon Sacco and the crew on the catch of a lifetime."
