Former Finance Minister Fikret Yusifov has previously argued that, if trade relations are restored, a trade deficit for Armenia would be inevitable, but that these economic ties should nevertheless be developed for the sake of peace.

There is also a widespread view among experts that food and beverages are psychologically more sensitive categories of goods. Construction materials, cable and electrical products, industrial raw materials, chemicals and light-industry goods, by contrast, may be perceived considerably more favourably.

Psychological barrier

This is one of the deepest and most sensitive aspects of the issue. Expert assessments published by Caliber note that memories of the 44-day war remain fresh. The appearance of products labelled Made in Armenia on shop shelves could initially provoke mixed reactions, ranging from curiosity to social media campaigns. Trust in food and beverages, including wine and brandy, is particularly important, as some consumers may have irrational concerns about their safety. With industrial goods and construction materials, by contrast, the country of origin is less visible to consumers and purchasing decisions tend to be more pragmatic.

During a transitional period, neutral packaging in English or Russian, or rebranding, could potentially be used. The appearance of Azerbaijani fuel on the Armenian market has already created a precedent for a kind of “economic truce”. A similarly pragmatic approach could work in the opposite direction, although this will not happen automatically.

In both societies, support for peace does not yet necessarily translate into an equally positive attitude towards goods from the neighbouring country. Traders from border areas who wished to remain anonymous, as well as entrepreneurs with experience of informal “re-exports” through Georgia using channels that have existed since the 1990s, say that price and quality could eventually become the decisive factors. However, this process could take years.

Practical obstacles and possible timeframes

Issues surrounding certification, phytosanitary controls, customs procedures, bank transfers and insurance have yet to be fully resolved.

Logistics currently operate mainly through Georgia. Direct rail links and the TRIPP corridor are still at the infrastructure development stage. Competition also remains high, with suppliers from Turkey, Russia and Iran already present in the market alongside domestic producers. The competitiveness of Armenian goods will therefore depend on their price, quality and logistics costs.

Under an optimistic scenario, small-scale shipments of industrial goods and raw materials could begin within several months to a year. A more realistic scenario would see trade gradually expand over one to three years, while under a pessimistic scenario, political fluctuations and public reaction could delay the process considerably.

What to watch next

Key indicators could include the first genuine commercial shipments from Armenia appearing in customs statistics, the introduction of banking mechanisms for cross-border payments, official approval of a list of potential goods for trade, and changes in the procurement policies of retailers such as Bravo, Araz and others.

Independent polling and sociological research in both countries will also be needed to assess public attitudes towards goods labelled “Made in …”. Without such data, statements about future trade will remain largely expressions of intent.

World.title: ‘From crisis management to stability’: Pashinyan unveils new government programme
World.content:
Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

The Armenian government has approved its programme for 2026-2031. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said it marked a shift from crisis management to stability. Looking back on his eight years as prime minister, he said the coronavirus pandemic, followed by the war and the post-war situation, had forced the government to operate in crisis-management mode. Now that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established peace, the government can “return to the unfinished part of the agenda of the 2018 Velvet Revolution”.

The new programme focuses on stability, he said. Pashinyan stressed that it rests entirely on the concept of “Real Armenia” and the principles underpinning the establishment of the Fourth Republic.

In 2025, the ruling Civil Contract party announced a new strategic goal: establishing the Fourth Republic of Armenia. The party congress unanimously adopted a declaration to this effect. According to the document, the Fourth Republic “will be based on the concept of preserving the internationally recognised sovereign territory of the Republic of Armenia, covering 29,743 sq km, in accordance with the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration”. The declaration says the party reached this decision after analysing the history of the Third Republic. The Third Republic refers to the present-day Republic of Armenia, which declared independence following a nationwide referendum in 1991. The First Republic refers to the republic proclaimed on 28 May 1918. Accordingly, Soviet Armenia is considered the Second Republic.

“Following the 7 June 2026 election, the ideology of ‘Real Armenia’ won. This means it has become the official ideology. Armenia is therefore entering the stage of its history that we call the Fourth Republic. We must continue and give new momentum to democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms,” the prime minister stressed.

Government plans for the next five years

According to the new programme, the Armenian government will pursue the following goals in 2026-2031:

strengthening and further institutionalising the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan;

maintaining and further developing a favourable security environment around Armenia, in particular by normalising and developing relations with countries in the region and deepening existing partnerships beyond it;

unblocking Armenia through the Crossroads of Peace project and the “Trump Route” (TRIPP) transit programme;

liberalising the visa regime with the EU for Armenian citizens;

deepening democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms.

With whom does Yerevan plan to deepen partnerships under its “balanced foreign policy”?

In 2026-2031, the Armenian government will pursue a “balanced and proportionate” foreign policy.

“It has proved effective in stabilising Armenia’s external environment. Regionalisation plays a key role in foreign policy, whose goal is to ensure conditions in which Armenia can not only live without external support, but do so comfortably,” the document says.

Based on this approach, the government places particular importance on further developing relations with Georgia, Iran, Turkey and Azerbaijan. The government has outlined the following steps for each neighbouring country:

Georgia

Yerevan will continue implementing the measures set out in the Declaration on Establishing a Strategic Partnership between Armenia and Georgia. This will create new mutually beneficial opportunities for political, trade, economic, energy and transport cooperation, as well as regional and joint infrastructure projects.

Iran

Armenia will continue energy cooperation with Iran, develop cross-border infrastructure and expand transport routes through Iran, including North-South and Persian Gulf-Black Sea corridors.

Turkey

The Armenian government will continue efforts to establish diplomatic relations with Turkey, open the Armenian-Turkish border and put at least two modern border crossing points into operation. It also plans to restore and expand transport, energy and digital infrastructure, as well as bilateral and multilateral trade.

Azerbaijan

The government plans to continue efforts to sign and ratify a peace agreement and carry out work on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. Contacts between civil society and business communities in the two countries will continue, helping to establish bilateral trade.

The foreign policy priorities specifically include deepening strategic partnerships with the European Union, the US, France and China. With Russia, Armenia plans to “transform and deepen its partnership”.

Against the backdrop of tensions over the ban on Armenian food and other exports to Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which Russia leads, the programme says:

“Work will continue to ensure the full and uninterrupted exercise of the EAEU’s fundamental freedoms — the free movement of labour, services, goods and capital — as well as to develop relations with member and observer states.”

Regarding relations with the European Union, the programme stresses that Armenia will continue working to meet standards in democracy and the rule of law, as well as in the economic, financial and other spheres.

Armenia intends to deepen its partnership with the United States further. Cooperation will continue based on the principles set out in the Strategic Partnership Charter and bilateral memorandums of understanding.

“The TRIPP project, the ‘Trump Route’, will be implemented, at least in terms of operating energy and railway infrastructure, while integrating Armenia into major regional infrastructure projects,” the programme says.

Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: Kazakhstan’s CEC holds media briefing ahead of Kurultai elections (PHOTO)
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 22. Kazakhstan’s Central Election Commission (CEC) held a briefing for foreign media representatives ahead of the upcoming elections to the Kurultai, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Astana.

CEC Deputy Chairman Yerman Mukhtar emphasized that the elections are being held within the established timeframe following the adoption of Kazakhstan’s new Constitution. “These are not early elections. These are elections being held within the established timeframe following the adoption of the new Constitution. This is very important,” he said.

During the briefing, CEC member Lyazzat Suyindik presented an overview of the new electoral system and the procedure for forming the Kurultai.

The Kurultai elections will be held under a proportional representation system, with deputies elected from party lists in a single nationwide electoral district. The new Kurultai will comprise 145 deputies elected for five-year terms. According to the CEC, Kazakhstan has 12,605,788 registered eligible voters. A total of 10,423 polling stations have been prepared, including 79 polling stations at 61 diplomatic missions and other locations abroad.

Accreditation of international observers officially closed on August 17, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. A total of 777 experts from 42 countries were registered to participate in election monitoring. Representatives of 13 international organizations are also taking part in the monitoring mission, including the OSCE, the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TurkPA) and other organizations.

On July 1, 2026, Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree setting August 23, 2026, as the date for the Kurultai elections.

Seven political parties are participating in the elections: Adilet, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, the Baitak Green Party of Kazakhstan, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Auyl, the Ak Zhol Democratic Party of Kazakhstan and Respublica.

World.title: Baku Mayor highlights role of $200B investments into city over 20 years
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 22. More than $200 billion in investment has been made in Baku over the past 20 years, Baku Mayor Eldar Azizov said at the fourth Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan Regional Forum in Tashkent, Trend's special correspondent reports.

“An interesting point: more than $200 billion has been invested in the city over the past 20 years. This process is continuing and gaining momentum,” Azizov said.

According to him, Baku continues to develop rapidly across a range of areas and is preparing for new urban development standards as a result of the policies pursued by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Azizov noted that Baku and its wider metropolitan area are now home to more than three million people. He also highlighted new examples of modern architecture in the city, including the Heydar Aliyev Center, Baku Olympic Stadium and the Flame Towers.

Azizov emphasized that Baku is not only a rapidly developing metropolis but also a platform for investment in urban infrastructure. “Most importantly, the city is safe. This safety is ensured not only by public order, cleanliness and an effective law enforcement system. Baku is also a safe city for investment in urban infrastructure,” he said.

The head of Baku’s executive authority invited representatives of Uzbek businesses to implement joint projects in the Azerbaijani capital. “We invite you to cooperate with us in our city and on our urban development platforms,” Azizov emphasized.

World.title: Baku-Tashkent cooperation gains momentum at city level – Baku Mayor
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 22. Cooperation between Baku and Tashkent is actively expanding, with interaction between the two capitals becoming increasingly regular, Baku Mayor Eldar Azizov said at the fourth Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan Regional Forum in Tashkent, Trend's special correspondent reports.

“Cooperation between our countries has reached a new level and is in many ways a model. The cities of the two countries are also part of this important process,” Azizov said.

He noted that his current visit to Tashkent was likely his fifth since taking office as head of Baku’s executive authority eight years ago. “An interesting point: I just realized that I have been working as head of Baku’s executive authority for eight years and this is probably my fifth visit to Tashkent. I think there is hardly another example that even comes close to this frequency. This also reflects the level of cooperation between our countries, cities and capitals,” Azizov said.

According to him, relations between Baku and Tashkent are developing actively within the framework of broader government-to-government cooperation, while meetings between city leaders and delegations at various levels have become regular.

Azizov said Baku has reached new development standards as a result of the policies pursued by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and has, in a sense, become a metropolis. “Today, the city and its wider agglomeration are home to more than three million people. It is developing rapidly, with new examples of modern architecture such as the Heydar Aliyev Center, Baku Olympic Stadium and the Flame Towers,” he said.

According to Azizov, Baku is preparing for the new standards of urban development, taking into account forecasts by futurists and scientists that the future of humanity will increasingly be concentrated in metropolitan areas.

In this context, and taking other factors into account, a new Master Plan for the development of Baku was prepared on the instructions of President Ilham Aliyev. “The Master Plan defines the city’s further development. Baku will become polycentric, which is particularly important given that the city stretches around 138 kilometers from one end to the other. It will be multifunctional and comfortable for its residents,” the mayor said.

He also spoke about projects aimed at developing new urban centers in Baku. In particular, Azizov highlighted the White City project, an area that had been heavily polluted during the Soviet period but was subsequently remediated. “On the initiative and instructions of President Ilham Aliyev, a completely new format was created. In fact, it is a city within a city,” he said.

Azizov also highlighted the successful implementation of the Sea Breeze project, noting that it has facilitated cooperation between Azerbaijani and Uzbek companies. “Overall, Baku continues to develop intensively across many areas. The city is developing and becoming cleaner, as many visitors to Azerbaijan have noted. And most importantly, the city is safe,” he said.

According to Azizov, Baku’s safety is ensured not only through public order, cleanliness and an effective law enforcement system, but also by creating reliable conditions for investment in urban infrastructure.

He invited Uzbek businesses to cooperate and implement projects in Baku. “In short, we invite you to cooperate with us in our city and on our urban development platforms. For our part, we promise to further strengthen our activities in our brother city of Tashkent. There are every reason to do so, and logic dictates that these relations should continue to develop,” Azizov emphasized.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections mark shift to practical functioning of new political system – deputy FM
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 22. The upcoming elections to Kazakhstan’s Kurultai mark the transition from constitutional decisions to the practical functioning of the country’s new political system, Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov said at a briefing for journalists ahead of the Kurultai elections, Trend’s special correspondent reports.

“Kazakhstan’s GDP grew by 6.5% in 2025. Industry, construction, transport, investment activity and other sectors made a significant contribution to this growth,” he said.

Issetov noted that Kazakhstan is steadily expanding the economic foundations of its development. Industrial production, infrastructure, transport and logistics, roads and the digital economy are developing, while investment is being attracted and new opportunities for businesses are being created. “However, economic development also presents the state with new challenges. The more complex the economy becomes, the more effective state institutions need to be. The greater the scale of private entrepreneurship and investment, the higher the requirements for the quality of legislation and public administration,” he said.

The deputy minister noted that as society becomes more diverse, it becomes increasingly important to have mechanisms that allow different public interests to be taken into account. “This is one of the main reasons behind the current constitutional reform. It is not aimed at change for the sake of change. Its purpose is to bring political institutions in line with modern Kazakhstan and prepare them for the country’s next stage of development. The upcoming Kurultai elections are an important part of this process. They mark the transition from constitutional decisions to the practical functioning of the new political system,” Issetov said.

On July 1, 2026, Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree setting August 23, 2026, as the date for elections to the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s unicameral parliament.

Previously, legislative power in Kazakhstan was exercised by a bicameral Parliament consisting of the Senate, the upper house, and the Mazhilis, the lower house. Under the new Constitution, which entered into force on July 1, 2026, Kazakhstan’s parliamentary system now provides for a unicameral Kurultai.

The Kurultai will comprise 145 deputies elected for five-year terms from party lists in a single nationwide electoral district through universal, equal and direct suffrage by secret ballot.

Seven political parties are participating in the elections: Adilet, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, the Baitak Green Party of Kazakhstan, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Auyl, the Ak Zhol Democratic Party of Kazakhstan and Respublica.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan sees sharp decline in number of social benefit recipients
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Kyrgyzstan sees sharp decline in number of social benefit recipients.

According to the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, this was presented at a meetingof the board of Kyrgyzstan’s Ministry of Labor, Social Security and Migration reviewing the ministry’s performance in the first half of 2026.

"At the board meeting, it was noted that, according to the National Statistical Committee, as of January 1, 2026, the number of benefit recipients decreased from 392,000 at the beginning of 2024 to 274,000 at the beginning of 2026," the board announced.

Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Ulan Mamatkanov, who attended the meeting, said the government needs to strengthen efforts to address poverty, unemployment, social assistance and labor migration.

At the same time, the government is expanding the social contract program, launched in 2022 on the initiative of President Sadyr Japarov. More than 48,000 families participated in the program between 2022 and 2025, while another 13,334 families are expected to join this year.

The ministry’s budget has also increased significantly, from 12 billion soms in 2021 to 25.4 billion soms in 2026.

Mamatkanov also highlighted ongoing reforms in the medical and social disability assessment system. The number of documents previously required for disability assessment has been reduced from six to two, while the system has been integrated with the Tunduk digital platform.

As a result, disability certificates and individual rehabilitation programs can now be obtained online.

He called for a comprehensive review of corruption risks across medical and social expert commissions and instructed officials to analyze complaints received in the regions over the past three years.

Mamatkanov also called for comprehensive inspections of all psycho-neurological and social residential institutions and stressed the need for state social service employees to treat citizens seeking assistance with respect and attention.

Meanwhile, in July 2026, the Bala Yrysy allowance was granted to 191,796 children, with 83% of payments processed electronically through a mobile application.

The meeting identified further priorities for the ministry, including improving social protection, employment support, labor rights protection and the efficiency of public services.

World.title: Seven killed in head-on collision with police car in UK
World.content:
Seven people, including two police officers, have died in a head-on collision in the north-east of England following a pursuit.

Police from Cleveland, Yorkshire - roughly 420kms north of London - said a Volkswagen Passat carrying five passengers was travelling the wrong way down the A66 highway near Middlesbrough when it collided head-on with a police vehicle.

All occupants of the Volkswagen and two police officers declared dead at the scene.

The police force said it was still investigating the circumstances of the crash and was working to formally identify all the people killed.

The families of those already identified have been informed and are being offered specialist support, police said.

"This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family," said Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller.

Local politician Anna Turley said Cleveland Police were investigating the incident, alongside the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

"It is crucial that we respect that process and avoid speculation at this deeply painful time," Ms Turley said.

The fatal crash follows two recent head-on crashes near Dublin, one of which killed five people.

Ireland's police chief this week warned that some young people were driving the wrong way on the motorway "for social media likes".

An Irish parliament committee has asked short-form video platform TikTok to explain how it removes content "that appears to glorify dangerous and illegal behaviour on our roads".

Ireland's media regulator made a similar request.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Ukraine strikes Russian retail warehouse in wave of drone attacks
World.content:
One day after a deadly 'double-tap' strike on a Ukranian shopping centre killed 16, Ukraine has fired back, hitting a Russian oil refinery as Moscow continues to take aim at civilian centres.

Moscow’s forces have intensified ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of US-made Patriot air defence interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one person was killed and another wounded in the latest attacks when the missiles hit railway infrastructure in the capital, Kyiv.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed its forces had hit a locomotive depot.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed a total of 457 Ukrainian drones overnight (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

In a separate attack, local authorities said two people were killed Saturday afternoon local time in a Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kyiv region, which surrounds the capital.

Russian drone strikes also killed four people and wounded another 15 in the Zaporizhzhia region, according to local officials.

President Zelenskyy said three people were also wounded in an attack on a minibus in the regional capital, also called Zaporizhzhia.

The United Nations said last week Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 wounded.

In the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said that two children had been killed and two adults wounded in a strike on the Sea of Azov port town of Yeysk.

He said a fire had broken out at an unnamed facility at the town's port.

The governor of Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, said two people had been killed and 13 wounded in Ukrainian attacks, with another four wounded in the nearby region of Bryansk.

In Luhansk, an eastern Ukrainian province almost all of which is controlled by Russia, Moscow-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said two civilians, including a 16-year-old boy, had been killed and nine more wounded.

Firefighters work at a site of a shopping centre hit by a Russian drones attack, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine. ( State Emergency Service of Ukraine via Reuters)

The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping centre in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine on Friday.

Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said the death toll had risen to 16 and nine people remain missing after the attack, which wounded another 130.

A site of a shopping centre hit by a Russian drones attack. (Telegram: Prosecutor General's Office)

Ukrainian strikes reach far behind enemy lines

Following the latest wave of Ukranian drone attacks, Russian online news outlet Astra reported an oil refinery in the country's Samara region had been set ablaze in a strike.

Mr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces struck the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Samara, noting its distance some 1,000 kilometres from the front line.

Ukraine has also cast a wider campaign against Russia's economic infrastructure, targeting online-retailer Ozon.

Ukraine's drone attacks on Russia could backfire Ukraine is firing drones deep inside Russian territory almost every day since June, but some analysts argue it could give Vladimir Putin an excuse to escalate his war.

In a statement on Telegram, Ozon said work at its Samara region logistics centre in the town of Chapayevsk had been halted after a strike, which it said caused injuries.

The strike is the first on Ozon, after weeks of drone attacks on its larger rival Wildberries.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed a total of 457 Ukrainian drones overnight.

ABC/WIRES

World.title: 'Lightning' the Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record
World.content:
A humanoid robot developed by Chinese smartphone maker Honor has beaten Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt's 100 metres world record at this year's World Humanoid Robot Games.

The robot — dubbed Lightning — ran 100 metres in 9.32 seconds and reached a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second during a preparatory test event for the games, China's state broadcaster reported on Saturday.

The performance surpassed the 9.58-second men's 100m world record set by Bolt at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin in 2009.

Lightning also won the 21-kilometre Beijing half marathon in April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the elite men's human world-record pace.

The robot stood 169 centimetres tall and had 95-centimetre legs at those games.

Researchers lengthened its legs by 10 centimetres ahead of the World Humanoid Robot Games which opened in Beijing on Saturday, China Central Television reported.

The 'Robot Olympics'

This year's World Humanoid Robot Games opened on Saturday. (Reuters: Florence Lo)

It's been called the Robot Olympics. But unlike the human Olympics, Team China is collecting almost all the medals.

Running from August 22 to 26, this year's World Humanoid Robot Games mark the second edition of the latest and biggest incarnation of China's robot games, which have been taking place for the past decade.

The 2026 games add a challenge for robotic hands, with robots judged on their speed and accuracy in precision tasks: tightening screws, opening bottles and picking up beads with tweezers.

The shift to work tasks in the games reflects the increasingly crowded industry's biggest problem: showing prototypes can work in the real world.

Robotic competitions in China have provided a window into the advances of a now surging sector — and the importance of its success as a strategic industry singled out by President Xi Jinping.

Once a curiosity organised by academic teams and hobbyists, China's robot games have become a national showcase celebrated by state media — and, increasingly, a proving ground for commercial products from companies looking to show real-world applications beyond the spectacle.

China has been promoting humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, with policymakers and companies betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their deployment in manufacturing, logistics and consumer applications.

Reuters

World.title: Thousands of Ervebo vaccine doses arrive in Ebola-stricken DRC
World.content:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo has received more than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine as the country grapples with the fastest Ebola outbreak in history, the country's health minister said.

The 16,250 doses arrived at N'djili International Airport in the capital, Kinshasa, late on Friday, the first of 70,000 doses expected from the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners that were announced on Thursday.

More doses are expected early next week.

The current Ebola outbreak in the DRC is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which currently has no approved treatment or vaccine.

It can spread easily and go undetected because some of its symptoms are similar to other illnesses, such as malaria.

The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to treat the Zaire strain of Ebola, and has been effective in past outbreaks. However, the WHO said it may provide some protection against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus.

Health workers are viewed with suspicion, all while they risk infection to help control the outbreak's spread. (Reuters: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere)

The latest outbreak, which has caused 2,557 deaths out of the 5,375 confirmed cases across six affected provinces, is spreading at an unprecedented rate, and is on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, which killed over 11,000 people across West Africa between 2014 and 2016.

Graphs show severity of Ebola outbreak The WHO's director-general says late-stage illness outside treatment centres and the unsafe handling of bodies after death are major drivers of transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The response to the outbreak has been hampered by difficulty contact tracing, hidden transmissions, regional instability threatening underpaid responders and difficulty corralling mass-movements.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows that transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three times its current rate.

Efforts to contain the outbreak have been made more difficult by armed conflict between the government and rebel groups, which control key cities in the hot spot; attacks on medical personnel and facilities; an itinerant labour population and people displaced by the armed conflict; and a lack of critical infrastructure.

AP

World.title: Zolani Tete shot dead outside his home in South Africa
World.content:
Former world boxing champion Zolani "Last Born" Tete has been shot dead outside his home in South Africa's Eastern Cape province, police and the country's sports minister said.

The 38-year-old was arriving at his residence in Mdantsane township when two armed men wearing balaclavas got out of a vehicle and opened fire.

"I will not speculate about who did this or why," Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said in a statement.

Tete's killing will renew attention on violent crime in South Africa, which continues to have one of the world's highest murder rates despite recent declines in homicides.

The killing was condemned by Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabunyane. (Reuters)

The murder of the world champion has also struck a chord in Mdantsane, the Eastern Cape township that has produced some of South Africa's most successful boxers.

SABC, the South African public broadcaster, reported that Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabuyane expressed shock and sadness at Tete's killing.

A spokesperson for the premier said: "It is heartbreaking that a life that brought so much pride to our province has been ended through such a brutal act of violence," according to SABC.

"We call on law enforcement agencies to leave no stone unturned to establish what happened and bring those responsible to book. Anyone with information must assist the police.

"On behalf of Premier Mabuyane and the EC provincial government, we extend our deepest condolences to the Tete family, his friends, the boxing fraternity and the community of Mdantsane.”

A woman travelling with Zolani Tete was also shot during the attack. (Reuters)

A 27-year-old woman travelling with Tete was shot multiple times and taken to hospital. Police have started investigations and the motive remains unclear.

Tete won the IBF junior bantamweight world title in 2014 after defeating Japan's Teiru Kinoshita in Kobe. He later won the WBO bantamweight crown.

He tested positive for the steroid stanozolol after a fight against British boxer Jason Cunningham in 2022 and was given a four-year suspension from competing, which expired in July this year.

He is best remembered internationally for his 11-second knockout of fellow South African Siboniso Gonya in Belfast in November 2017, the fastest stoppage in a world title fight.

Reuters

World.title: Mackay makes cricket history as day one of inaugural Test match sells out
World.content:
Barry Jansen mortgaged his house to help buy land for a cricket arena and didn't tell his wife for five years.

More than 40 years later, history is being made on the same field as the Queensland city of Mackay hosts its first international Test cricket match.

Mr Jansen said in the late 1980s the cricket association wanted to expand but needed financial backing.

Three members took an extraordinary personal risk and mortgaged their homes to help make it happen.

"We couldn't afford to pay our groundsmen without extending our facility. We didn't have the finance. We had park land with some value and that was all," he said.

Mackay cricket stalwart Barry Jansen in the commentary box. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

A government grant and a bank loan guaranteed by three members' homes helped fund the expansion.

Mr Jansen said there were a "couple of quiet moments" about five years later when he told his wife he'd mortgaged their home.

"I was very, very fortunate. I always say, it [Harrup Park] is like one of the family," he said.

"My wife always says it was part of the family because we'd sunk so much in it."

Nicolas Jones and Joe Brayshaw are on safari from Brisbane for the test. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

In 1939 the field was a cow paddock, purchased by local farmers for 1,000 pounds to start a cricket club.

"It was definitely a risk but those people then created the vision and we had to do it," Mr Jansen said.

'True cricket lovers'

Grandstands and hills at Harrup Park's Great Barrier Reef Arena were packed out with Bangladeshi locals waving flags and placards, with a "tiger" or two in the mix.

Shagufta Hasan, who described herself as a "true cricket lover", said Mackay's Bangladeshi community was cricket obsessed.

Members of Mackay's Bangladeshi community were out in force to support their team. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

"It doesn't matter if Bangladesh are playing or not, we're always watching," she said.

"We have 32 Bangladeshi families in Mackay so when the news came we all are very excited."

Scoring dream

Mackay resident Mel Dwyer, one of two Cricket Australia official scorers at the game, said it was a dream come true to score a Test in her home town.

She made her Test scoring debut at the Gabba in 2024 for Australia vs West Indies.

Mel Dwyer says scoring a Test match in her home town of Mackay was a dream come true. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Matches are scored on paper and she said the slower pace of a Test made the job "a little bit easier" than a T20 match.

"There are plenty of sets of eyes watching and there's lots of talking going on as far as what happens with every ball. We have to confirm everything," she said.

Ms Dwyer started scoring about 12 years ago when her youngest child started playing representative cricket.

"I just put my hand up to help out with those games because I found that if I sat on the sideline with the other parents, I would be too engrossed in conversations with them and miss what was actually going on the field," she said.

Cricket fans from Sydney flew in for the test match. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Ms Dwyer grew up in a family of cricket lovers in a house full of memorabilia celebrating Sir Donald Bradman and the Invincibles.

"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would be working in cricket and scoring Test matches. A five-day test match would be absolutely amazing," she said.

Strong pitch

Peter Kazakoff, head curator of Great Barrier Reef Arena, said perfect weather and just the right amount of rain earlier in the week combined for a strong pitch.

The wicket in Mackay has the same clay soil profile as the Gabba.

"We source it from the same paddock down in Peak Crossing just at the back of Ipswich," he said.

Mr Kazakoff said selectors, coaches and players had been "blown out of the water" by the playing surface.

"We've gone from being a country cricket ground to an international test cricket venue. It's quite remarkable."

World.title: Sydney childcare centre on brink of closure offered 12-months rent free
World.content:
An inner Sydney childcare centre on the brink of closure has been handed a lifeline, as parents fight to keep the doors open.

Goodstart Early Learning has announced plans to shut its east Sydney service in Darlinghurst on November 26, blaming high costs, prompting a petition to save it.

The not-for-profit, which rents the site from the City of Sydney, said the centre was making a "significant loss" despite high occupancy.

It said the centre needed more staff to supervise children as it was spread over multiple levels.

Parents rally to show their support for the centre. (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

In addition, the provider said the federal government had rejected its request to raise its fees beyond a current cap of $175 per day.

In response to the uproar, council offered the early learning centre 12 months free rent while its future is resolved.

"I hope this gives comfort and certainty to parents that we are committed to ensuring stability and the learning community they have built in Darlo [Darlinghurst]," Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore said on social media.

The provider, which leases three other sites from the City of Sydney, is yet to say whether it has accepted the rent waiver.

The ABC has reached out for comment.

'There aren't many options in the area'

On Saturday, Tim Martin was among parents who rallied at Kings Cross to save the centre.

"Losing the centre would be so devastating," the father-of-two said.

"What we really feel for is the staff of the centre too, they probably won't have jobs."

Mr Martin says losing the centre would be "devastating". (ABC News)

Mr Martin said he and his wife had already canvassed close to six centres nearby.

"They're all full, some have a day here or there, but it's just not doable."

Goodstart closed two other centres earlier this year at Bondi Junction.

Another not-for-profit in Paddington could also be lost as the site is earmarked to be sold.

Fiona Thatcher said her 11-month-old daughter Mave had been on the centre's waiting list since she was in the womb.

"I don't think many of us have much of a plan B because there aren't many options in the area at all," she said.

"It would certainly involve enrolling in multiple centres, driving quite a distance … it would also mean losing the educators, which was the primary motivators for getting together like this."

Ms Thatcher says there are not many childcare options in the area. (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

Ms Thatcher said she did not think the area could accommodate the 60 families enrolled at the childcare centre and the more than 100 on its waiting list.

Labor Councillor Zann Maxwell said the demand was there, but the provider had given "mixed messages" about the site's closure.

"The last thing we want to see is the loss of a childcare centre in the inner-city," he said.

"We want to be making sure that this is the kind of place where all sorts of people can live, including young families, and we're not serious about it if we let places like this close."

Cr Maxwell said if the Goodstart centre could not survive, the City of Sydney should step in and run its own centre in the area.

The council already owns and operates four centres.

World.title: Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
World.content:
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike

Mitchell Starc claimed a first ball wicket in both of this first two overs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.

Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.

Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.

He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.

Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.

England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.

And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.

Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.

2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls

Mitchell Starc tore through the top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.

Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.

Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.

But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.

Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.

And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.

It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.

It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.

It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.

3. Obstructing the field?

Hazlewood was unimpressed with Taskin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.

Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.

Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.

Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.

The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.

Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.

There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.

Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.

Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.

4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return

Renshaw was dimissed cheaply on his return to the Test arena. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.

The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.

He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.

And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.

The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.

Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.

5. Shoriful's dream day

The towering Shoriful made an instant impact at the bowling crease. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.

The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.

Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.

Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.

Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.

This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.

And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.

First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.

Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

World.title: The next time you check into a hotel, you might not need a key
World.content:
Travel newsAustralia The next time you check into a hotel, you might not need a key Julietta Jameson August 23, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was a time when checking into a hotel meant being handed an actual key, often attached to a hefty fob designed to discourage guests from accidentally taking it home. You might even have had to hand it in at reception when leaving your digs temporarily. Hold the phone – mobile phone room keys are here. Though heritage and boutique properties might still offer them, the metal key largely disappeared decades ago, replaced by a plastic or, increasingly, some kind of sustainable-material key card. Now those, too, could be on their way out. Guests at QT Sydney can now access their rooms using a digital key stored in their Apple or Google wallet, following the launch of new technology by EVT Hotels & Resorts. The Australian hotel group, which owns and operates brands including QT, Rydges, Atura and LyLo, says it is the first multi-brand hotel group in Australia to introduce mobile wallet hotel keys across its portfolio. With QT Sydney as the forerunner, the technology will be rolled out across the four brands over the next year.



The QT Sydney room key. 



Parlour at QT Sydney has kept the original glass vitrines of Gowings department store – not everything changes. Hyatt was an early adopter, launching Room Keys in Apple Wallet at six US hotels in 2021. But the technology is now moving towards a much broader digital access system. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Why hotel check-in still takes forever – but doesn’t have to Michael Gebicki The Tripologist In February the global Connectivity Standards Alliance released Aliro 1.0, a new digital access standard backed by Apple, Google and Samsung. Designed to allow phones and smartwatches to work across compatible access systems, rather than relying on proprietary technology, Aliro specifically includes hotels among its intended uses. For hotel operators, however, the appeal isn’t simply saving guests the trouble of carrying another piece of plastic. Physical key cards have to be purchased, encoded, replaced when they’re lost and ultimately disposed of. And how many of us have arrived home with one still in the bottom of a bag?



Digital keys potentially reduce those costs as well as plastic and e-waste. EVT says reducing its reliance on cards is part of the rationale for its rollout. Security is another consideration. Digital credentials can be remotely deactivated and, unlike a loose hotel key card, sit within the security architecture of the guest’s phone. Issuing a digital key doesn’t necessarily remove the need for reception. Identity verification, payment and individual hotel procedures can still require guests to check in with staff. But those processes are changing, too. Apple already allows participating hotels to incorporate check-in and room assignment into the Wallet experience, potentially allowing guests to arrive with their room key already on their phone and head directly to their rooms. That makes EVT’s rollout interesting beyond the novelty of opening a hotel door with a watch. Hotels have spent years digitising booking, payment, check-out, restaurant ordering and communication with guests. EVT, like many others, already offers online check-in, guest messaging, mobile payments and in-room dining ordering.



The humble room key is one of the remaining pieces of the hotel stay still routinely handed across a desk. For how long? Well, there is still reason not to write the obituary for the hotel key card just yet. Not every guest owns a compatible device or wants to use one – and hotels still need alternatives when technology fails. See evt.com

World.title: Preston in hospital on drip before Bulldogs game, five players with Covid
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Preston in hospital on drip before Bulldogs game, five players with Covid Chris Barrett August 22, 2026 — 11:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Canterbury have kept alive their slim finals hopes despite back-rower Jacob Preston spending two days in hospital on a drip, five players contracting Covid-19 and winger Jacob Kiraz secretly playing with a torn calf for the past three weeks. In yet another pre-match disruption, centre Matt Burton missed training in the lead-up to Saturday night’s must-win clash with St George Illawarra to return home to Dubbo for a family issue. Jacob Preston and the Bulldogs celebrate a try on Saturday night. Getty Images And before kick-off, Enari Tuala was ruled out with a knee injury which he aggravated at training. As far as preparations go, it is hard to envisage there being more interruptions.



The Bulldogs, however, performed as if it had been plain sailing for them all week, beating the Dragons 44-14 in a free-flowing and clinical display before a crowd of 14,711 at Allianz Stadium. The victory leaves the ninth-placed side two points behind South Sydney and North Queensland with two matches remaining. They still need results to go in their favour to make the top eight and their penultimate opponents of the regular season, Penrith, will present a steeper challenge next Friday night at CommBank Stadium. Loading But Canterbury will approach the round 26 blockbuster in the knowledge that they were the first team to beat the Panthers this season and with renewed verve after taking care of St George Illawarra comfortably.



The fact that they did so after the week they had - and following a deflating last-start defeat to South Sydney - was another vote of confidence. “These things happen in a footy season. Every team goes through them. A lot of them you don’t hear about,” Bulldogs coach Cameron Ciraldo said. “I was a bit harsh on the boys last week, and then you rock up Monday and about five of them have tested positive for COVID, so no wonder they were a bit flat.” On top of that, Preston, who has been in high-profile contract negotiations with the club, had been hospitalised ahead of the contest with an injection in his elbow. “So he was on a trip over the last couple of days,” Ciraldo said.



Not done with the post-game revelations, the coach then let slip that Kiraz had been quietly playing with a tear in his calf, having incurred the same injury on his other leg earlier this season. Burton, meanwhile, switched from left to right centre to accommodate the return of Bronson Xerri after having to skip training for family reasons. Along with Preston, he was a standout with a pair of tries and some try-saving defence. “I just feel like it balanced the team up a little bit,” Ciraldo said of Burton’s shift to the right. “Burto wanted that challenge of going on Val Holmes. They’re both Origin players and I think Burto was pretty excited by that.”



Related Article Match report The Warriors can challenge for the title. Souths need Latrell back to stand a chance In an impressive all-round outing, Burton and Preston were in good company. Xerri, making his first start in six weeks, demonstrated what he can provide to Canterbury before he heads to Melbourne next season with a try of his own, while halfback Lachlan Galvin scored one and set up two. A busy Jaeman Salmon and Bailey Hayward were other top performers while Ciraldo credited fullback Connor Tracey with his best game of the year. With Tuala due back next week, the only concerns for Canterbury as they turn their attention to Penrith were Salmon being placed on report twice and a groin injury that forced utility Kurt Mann off the field in the second half. They were too strong for the Dragons despite two periods in which they were reduced to 12 men.



Dean Young’s team gave a better account than the scoreline suggested but were undone by mistakes. They also lost hooker Jacob Liddle with a suspected torn calf. There were concerns the 29-year-old had ruptured his achilles, but those fears were eased by Dragons medical staff. “I hope it is just a calf,” said departing captain Damien Cook, who replaced Liddle when Liddle went off at the half-hour mark. “I was pretty worried for him. He’s someone I’ve enjoyed working along with. He’s been playing really good footy of late. He deserves to be starting and he’s going to do a great job for the team next year.”



The result snapped a two-game winning run for St George Illawarra and all but assured they will collect the wooden spoon. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Wildcards locked in: Blues, Pies, Demons and Dogs learn their fate for history-making round
World.content:
Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Carlton CEO Graham Wright opened up on the future of Elijah Hollands on the day their wildcard opponent was locked in.

Scott Pendlebury and Brayden Maynard are both set to miss the Pies’ wildcard clash with the Bulldogs. Elijah Hollands could have played his final game for us: Carlton CEO By Danny Russell and Russell Bennett Carlton chief executive Graham Wright doubts Elijah Hollands will return to play for the club as the Blues set their sights on a remarkable wildcard final against Melbourne. Wright was speaking before Carlton’s barnstorming win against ladder leader Fremantle at Marvel Stadium, a victory that sees Josh Fraser’s side hit the finals series with undeniable momentum. The Blues, who finished the home-and-away season in 10th, will now face the 7th-placed Demons in one wildcard final next week, while the Bulldogs will host Collingwood in the other.



Elijah Hollands suffered a mental health episode during a game early this season. AFL Photos Hollands, the 24-year-old midfielder-forward, hasn’t played at any level since round six of the AFL season, when he experienced a mental health episode on the field against Collingwood at the MCG. The Blues were later fined $75,000 for bringing the game into disrepute over their handling over the matter in April after the AFL said Hollands should have been removed from the field earlier than he was, citing visual clues, performance data during the match, and knowledge of his individual circumstances. “These findings have been made against the Carlton Football Club collectively, not against any individual,” league CEO Andrew Dillon said in a press conference in May. Speaking on 3AW on Saturday, Wright was asked directly if he thought Hollands would return to play at the club.



“I doubt it,” he said, adding that Hollands continues to receive support. Hollands (right) with then-Blues coach Michael Voss after the loss to Collingwood. AFL Photos “That’s coming through the club, but also, too, wider than that,” he said. “He hasn’t been back to the club, and he’s considering what he does, but certainly we’re just trying to be there and support him. “We’ll work out what that looks like from a futuristic point of view a little bit later on.”



The Blues fell four goals behind against the Dockers in the opening 12 minutes on Saturday, looking slow, outnumbered and second-rate. That’s when the Fraser way took hold. They rallied to close to within three points at the first break, led by 11 points at half-time and then dominated the second half to win 18.11 (119) to 12.10 (82). They had 114 more disposals and 56 more marks. The key to the early turnaround, midfield star Sam Walsh revealed, was “not making it a bit a bigger deal than it needed to be”. View post on X “At the moment, we’re probably assessing what’s not working and changing in game, which has been a growth,” he told The Age.



Carlton’s growth since round 10 was enormous. They had a devastating 1-8 start to the season and a series of second-half fadeouts that cost Michael Voss his job. They were continually hamstrung by the absence of a Plan B. Not any more. Under Fraser, they have catapulted themselves into the wild card round with an ominous momentum, winning 11 of their final 14 matches of the home-and-away season. But did they ever think finals were possible? “No, we couldn’t have,” Walsh said. “But the best thing we have done is that we didn’t even speak of getting to that point.



“Like we focus on, when Frase took over, what do we want to stand for? And then, from there, how do we get after it every week?” Getting after it was second nature for Walsh on Saturday. He was again outstanding. He had 32 possessions and kicked a goal against Fremantle to marginally shade boy wonder Jagga Smith, who helped himself to 31 disposals and also booted a major. Harry McKay with the Blues faithful after stunning the Dockers at Marvel Stadium. AFL Photos But it was the performance of the lesser lights under Fraser that helped the Blues climb into the finals. Cult hero Frankie Evans booted five goals against the Dockers, Gold Coast recruit Ben Ainsworth managed three and former Sydney rebound defender Ollie Florent was instrumental in their attacking thrusts, amassing 29 disposals at Marvel Stadium in their final home-and-away game.



Even the returned Ollie Hollands had an opportunity to shine. He brought the Carlton faithful to their feet with an inspiring run-down tackle on super villain Patrick Voss that saved a certain goal. But despite this growing adulation and rising expectation from the success-starved Blues army, there was no way the new Blues coach would allow the lid to come off. That was old Carlton. “I think the context of where we’ve come from, and maybe the context of the club more broadly, that maybe in the past it’s been outcome-based,” Fraser said. “Maybe I’m speculating a little bit because I haven’t really lived it. But we’ve got a method right now that is working for us, and I think if we stray too far away from that, then there’s some danger attached to it as well.” Fraser was right. While the Blues had beaten flag favourites Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions in the past month, there were caveats attached to those wins, especially on Saturday.



The Dockers were not at their best. They left Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and Sam Switkowski in Perth. They also treated their bench like a game of musical chairs, constantly managing the game time of their biggest names – Luke Jackson, Caleb Serong, Alex Pearce and Shai Bolton. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir said he was disappointed in the loss, but he was hardly convincing. “I thought we got out of it pretty well in terms of what we wanted to do with minimising risk and game time,” Longmuir said. View post on X



The low point for the Dockers was losing Brennan Cox with a calf injury that will rule him out of their first final in a fortnight. “There was a lot of moving parts today in terms of the team we picked, who we left out, and then Coxy going down didn’t help,” Longmuir said. “But we’ll put it behind us pretty quickly, and reflect on the season. And we should have really good belief [going forward].” The Blues stand to regain Nick Haynes and Will Hayward next week, and were able to rest key defender Jacob Weitering for a large slice of the final term. Pendlebury’s playing future clouded following injury



By Jon Pierik Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week against the Bulldogs and could well have played his final match in black and white. The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder (on 442) had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”. Will Ashcroft and Scott Pendlebury after their blockbuster clash on Friday night. AFL Photos In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also miss their wildcard clash against the Western Bulldogs next week.



The Bulldogs have a worry of their own. Despite a courageous 21-point win over Melbourne at the MCG to hold on to eighth place, the Dogs will sweat on an ankle injury to key forward Aaron Naughton, who hobbled from the ground after landing heavily in a marking contest. View post on X The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper. “These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon. “Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks.



Related Article AFL 2026 The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers “Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury. “These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.” Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend, and 1990 Collingwood premiership coach, Leigh Matthews said it would be wrong for Collingwood to allow Pendlebury to make his own call on his playing future, declaring the Magpies needed to deliver honest feedback. Pendlebury, 38, finished the clash against the Lions with what was initially thought to be a knee bursa issue (swelling near the joint).



He is set to become an unrestricted free agent, with several clubs linked to his services if he opts to play elsewhere in 2027. Magpies president Barry Carp said on Friday night that the choice was in Pendlebury’s hands, but Matthews said any decision should largely be the club’s call. “Not in my opinion, it’s never the player’s call,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday. “But Scott Pendlebury is a high-class person. If [coach] Craig McRae and the football people said: ‘We think it’s probably time’, I think he would accept that. And that’s the way the conversation should go. “But a player just can’t say, ‘I want to play, I don’t care if you don’t think I am up to it, I just want to play and I want a contract.’



“But even Barry Carp, I don’t think he would go that far. I think if the football department said: ‘No, we just think it’s time’, I probably suspect Scott Pendlebury would accept that himself. “It’s a joint conversation, but it can’t be unilaterally [that] the player decides, otherwise he would play until he is 50.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
